title: Good tidings of great joy (Luke 2:8–20)
hook: the angel to the shepherds: fear not, a savior is born
tomorrow: now let me go in peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, in those days: an emperor counting the world, and a baby laid in a manger at its edge. Your line was not counted, but there. Who did the headline miss today? Day five hundred nine.

Night shift. Out in the fields near Bethlehem, a few shepherds are keeping watch over their flock. It's cold, it's dark, and the job is mostly staying awake: listening for wolves, counting sheep, the original night watchmen. Not people anyone would invite to a palace. Not people the emperor's census was thinking about. And then, in the King James Bible: "the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid." Sore afraid. Terrified. The dark field suddenly blazing. And the first words, as with Zechariah and Mary, are the same two words.

"Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord." Every word is loaded. Good tidings is one Greek verb, the root of the word gospel: to announce good news. Emperors used that kind of language for their birthdays and victories. Here it comes to shepherds, about a baby. To all people: not just the important ones. This day: Luke's favorite word, today. And the sign isn't a palace or a crown. "Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger." The sign is how ordinary he is. Then the sky fills with angels singing: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." That line became the Gloria, sung in churches for many centuries. And here's a curiosity: ancient manuscripts differ here by a single letter. Some read peace, good will toward men. Others read peace among people with whom God is pleased. Translations follow different manuscripts, and the meaning shifts a little either way. Then the shepherds do the simplest thing: "Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see." They find everything just as they were told, and they tell everyone, and people are amazed. And then a quiet line about Mary: "But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart." The shepherds broadcast. Mary treasures. Both are ways of receiving good news. The shepherds go back to their fields, the text says, glorifying and praising God. Same job, same sheep, same cold night. Changed.
screen: `THE SIGN IS HOW ORDINARY HE IS.`
then, large: `GOOD TIDINGS OF GREAT JOY, TO ALL PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell someone good news. Settle, and breathe. First, find some. Not the big kind, necessarily. Something good that's actually true: a friend's recovery, a kindness you saw, a baby born, a small win at work, a thing you're grateful for. Let it come up and sit with it, the way Mary pondered. Then think of who needs to hear it. Someone who's been surrounded by bad news lately. Someone who'd smile. Picture telling them, the way the shepherds did, a little breathless, not polished. If you pray, you can give thanks for the good news first. If you don't, simply enjoy it before you share it. The bell holds the time.
Good tidings of great joy. The angel's announcement to shepherds on the night shift: a savior born, this day, for all people.

segments.voice: Your line: great joy for all people. Today, tell someone the good news you found, and let your face show it. Day five hundred nine.

howItsDone: Christians read the shepherds' story on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, and the angels' song lives on in the Gloria, sung or said in many churches' Sunday worship and in many Christmas carols.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty line from a Christmas card.
what it means: good news announced to night-shift shepherds, for all people, with a sign as ordinary as a baby in a feeding trough.
what a scholar hears: Luke 2:14's manuscripts differ by one letter, so the angels sing either good will toward men or peace among people God favors.

notes: Luke 2:14 variant: eudokia (nominative, 'good will toward men', Byzantine text behind the KJV) vs eudokias (genitive, 'among men of good will / with whom he is pleased', older manuscripts). Confirm the 'single letter' description.
Imperial use of 'good news' (euangelion) language, e.g. the Priene inscription on Augustus's birthday. Stated generally.
Shepherds' social status: the script avoids claiming they were despised (debated); says only 'not people anyone would invite to a palace'.
